title_en: Fragment from the Commentary on Hosea
author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen addresses a textual difficulty in Hosea where plural verbs shift to a singular, because some readers suspect an error and alter the wording. He explains the apparent solecism by showing that Scripture deliberately uses singular and plural to teach about unity with God.
argument: Origen argues that the shift from plural to singular in Hosea is not a scribal error but a deliberate scriptural pattern. He shows from Genesis that God addresses Adam in the singular when commanding what leads to life, but in the plural when warning about transgression. The many who seek God become one when they find him and hear his word, while the one who sins becomes many by falling away from unity. He supports this with apostolic texts and the Shepherd of Hermas, all teaching that the faithful are one body in Christ.

outline.move: Origen introduces the problem: apparent grammatical inconsistency in Hosea where plural verbs are followed by a singular, and some readers wrongly correct the text.
He cites the Hosea passage and compares it with God's command to Adam in Genesis, where singular and plural are similarly mixed.
He explains the principle: the many who walk according to God are one, so the singular is used for the good command and for finding God, while the plural is used for transgression.
He confirms the principle with apostolic texts, the Savior's prayer, and the Shepherd of Hermas, showing that the saints are one body and one in Christ.

key_terms.sense: Apparently ungrammatical or inconsistent wording in Scripture
Correction of the biblical text by readers who think it is faulty
Grammatical singular, used when the many are united with God
Grammatical plural, used for transgression or before unity is achieved
Being of one mind, the state that makes many into one
The unity from which the sinner falls and to which the faithful are joined
The one body that the many believers are in Christ
The building of the tower in the Shepherd of Hermas, symbolizing the unity of many stones into one
The harmony of many that constitutes unity

scripture: Origen uses the Septuagint (LXX) text and its book names. Hosea is cited as 'Osee'. Genesis is cited as 'Genesis'. The apostolic quotations are heavily adapted or paraphrased combinations rather than direct citations of a standard text-type. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names.
uncertain: The exact date of the commentary's composition is not stated in the fragment.
The precise biblical text of Hosea Origen used cannot be fully reconstructed from the fragment.
The identity of the addressee is not indicated in the surviving text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He shows from Genesis that God addresses Adam in the singular when commanding what leads to life, but in the plural when warning about transgression.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀρξάμενος γὰρ κἀκεῖ ἀπὸ ἑνικοῦ ἐν τῷ εἰρηκέναι, παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φαγῇ, ἐπιφέρει πληθυντικῶς, εἰπὼν, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν, οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen shows from Genesis that God addresses Adam with a singular verb (φαγῇ) for the positive command about eating from every tree, but shifts to plural verbs (φάγεσθε, φάγητε, ἀποθανεῖσθε) for the prohibition and warning about death. The shift is in verb number, not in the addressee (Adam remains singular throughout).

_unresolved_facts.claim: the many who seek God become one when they find him and hear his word
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅτε ἔτι κλαίουσι καὶ δέονται πρὸς Θεόν, πληθυντικῶς λέγεται τὸ, Ἔκλαυσαν καὶ ἐδεήθησαν· ὅτε δὲ εὑρίσκουσι τὸν Θεόν, οὐκέτι πληθυντικῶς φησι τὸ, Ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτούς, ἀλλὰ, πρὸς αὐτόν. Ἤδη γὰρ ἐν γεγόνασιν οἱ πολλοὶ ἐν τῷ εὑρηκέναι τὸν Θεόν, καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀκούειν λόγον αὐτοῦ.
_unresolved_facts.fix: the many who weep and pray to God become one when they find him and hear his word

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πληθυντικῶς γὰρ εἰπὼν, Ἔκλαυσαν καὶ ἐδεήθησάν μου· καὶ πάλιν πληθυντικῶς τὸ ἑξῆς δηλώσας, Ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ὢν, εὗρόν με, τὸ ἑξῆς ἐπὶ ἑνικοῦ ἐπιφέρει, λέγων· Καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτόν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ['frag-open'] — the Hosea quotations appear only in frag-open; in frag-rem-early Origen refers back to the Hosea text with εἴποι ἂν but does not re-quote it as fresh Hosea speech

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐν τῇ Γενέσει ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἀδὰμ ἐντολὴν διδοὺς, οὕτω φησίν· Ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φαγῇ
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ['frag-rem-early', 'frag-rem-mid'] — the Genesis quotation is split: the initial citation appears in frag-rem-early, but Origen continues to quote and discuss it in frag-rem-mid (βρώσει φαγῇ; Οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καθὼς καὶ ὁ Ἀπόστολος μαρτυρεῖ, εἰπών· Ὅτι εἷς ἄρτος καὶ ἓν σῶμα οἱ πολλοί ἐσμεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the Apostle (quoted Scripture) ... with direct quotation introduced by εἰπών

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πάτερ γὰρ, φησὶν, ἅγιε, δὸς ἵνα, καθὼς ἐγὼ καὶ σὺ ἕν ἐσμεν, οὕτω καὶ οὗτοι ἐν ἡμῖν ἓν ὦσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Jesus (quoted Scripture) ... the source gives a direct quotation introduced by φησὶν, closely following John 17:21 though with some adaptation
